title: PRC NDLE 2021 - Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietetics
description: Official 200-question Board Licensure Examination (Oct 17, 2021, Set A) covering Clinical Dietetics, MNT, Nutritional Biochemistry, and Hospital Dietetics.

cards.front: Diet-related components that may be protective against CHD include all of the following, EXCEPT:
options: A. antioxidant nutrients, particularly vit. E
cards.rationale: Cardioprotective dietary components include antioxidant nutrients like Vitamin E (which inhibits LDL oxidation), soluble fiber (which binds bile acids and lowers serum total and LDL cholesterol), and B-vitamins such as folate, B6, and B12 (which lower circulating homocysteine, an independent vascular risk factor). Vitamin K functions primarily in hepatic synthesis of blood clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) and bone mineralization (osteocalcin carboxylation), and is not classified as a CHD-protective nutrient.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. Vitamin K. Margin: CHD protective nutrients include Vit E (antioxidant), fiber (bile binding), folate (homocysteine reduction).

cards.front:
Characteristics of objectives must be:
I. Specific and patient centered
II. Time bound
III. Realistic
IV. Measurable
cards.back: B. I, II, III and IV
options: B. I, II, III and IV
cards.rationale: In Medical Nutrition Therapy and nutrition counseling, goal-setting follows the SMART framework: Specific, Measurable, Attainable/Realistic, Relevant/Patient-centered, and Time-bound. Thus, all Roman numerals I, II, III, and IV are essential characteristics of sound clinical objectives.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B (I, II, III and IV). SMART criteria in clinical nutrition care plans.

cards.front: The serving portion of each food on any given list provide the same amount of:
cards.rationale: In the Food Exchange Lists (Exchange System / PEL), foods are grouped into lists based on similarity in macronutrient composition (carbohydrates, proteins, fats). Consequently, any serving portion within a given exchange list yields approximately the same amount of energy (calories).
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. energy. Margin: Exchange system groups foods by equivalent macronutrients and caloric energy.

cards.front: The situation following or resulting from a behavior is called the:
cards.rationale: In behavioral modification and cognitive-behavioral theory, the ABC framework consists of Antecedents (stimuli, triggers, or cues occurring prior to behavior), Behavior (the action itself), and Consequences (the events, responses, or outcomes that follow and reinforce or extinguish the behavior).
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. Consequences. ABC Model: Antecedent -> Behavior -> Consequence.

cards.front: Which strategy is safe for increasing the energy intake of people on fat-restricted diets?
cards.back: D. provide additional fat in the form of MCT oil
options: A. gradually add fat as tolerance permits
B. provide fat with enzymes replacements
D. provide additional fat in the form of MCT oil
cards.rationale: Medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs, C6-C12) do not require micellar emulsification by bile salts or hydrolysis by pancreatic lipase. They are rapidly absorbed directly into enterocytes and transported via the portal venous circulation directly to the liver. This makes MCT oil safe and calorie-dense (8.3 kcal/g) for patients with severe fat malabsorption or pancreatitis on fat-restricted diets.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. Provide additional fat in the form of MCT oil. MCT oil bypasses lymphatic chylomicron transport.

cards.front: Which is considered as fuel for the gut?
cards.rationale: Glutamine is the principal, preferred oxidative fuel source for rapidly dividing enterocytes of the small intestine and colonocytes, as well as mucosal lymphocytes. It is critical for maintaining intestinal mucosal barrier integrity and preventing bacterial translocation during physiologic stress.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. Glutamine. Margin: Fuel of enterocytes = Glutamine; Fuel of colonocytes = Short-chain fatty acids (butyrate).

cards.front: Nutrition concerns most commonly associated with chronic gastritis include:
options: C. delayed gastric emptying and pernicious anemia
D. iron-deficiency anemia and protein malabsorption
cards.rationale: Chronic atrophic gastritis (especially autoimmune Type A gastritis targeting parietal cells) causes progressive loss of gastric acid (achlorhydria) and intrinsic factor secretion. Lack of intrinsic factor prevents Vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum, culminating in pernicious anemia. Chronic dyspepsia, anorexia, and malabsorption also contribute to generalized malnutrition.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. malnutrition and pernicious anemia. Note: Loss of parietal cells -> decreased intrinsic factor -> pernicious anemia.

cards.front: A sodium-restricted diet may be ordered for clients with _____.
cards.rationale: In Congestive Heart Failure (CHF), decreased cardiac output triggers renal hypoperfusion and compensatory activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), promoting massive sodium and fluid retention (pulmonary congestion and peripheral edema). Sodium restriction (typically 2,000 mg/day) is a cornerstone of MNT to prevent hypervolemia.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. congestive heart failure. Margin note connects sodium restriction to edema and CHF management.

cards.front:
Which of the following will you advise a patient who is suffering from peptic ulcer?
I. No smoking
II. Avoid taking aspirin
III. Diet should be caffeine free
IV. Take a liberal bland diet
cards.back: A. I, II, III and IV
options: A. I, II, III and IV
cards.rationale: Comprehensive MNT and lifestyle advice for Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD) includes: smoking cessation (nicotine impairs mucosal blood flow and bicarbonate secretion), eliminating aspirin/NSAIDs (which inhibit protective prostaglandin synthesis), avoiding caffeine and decaffeinated coffee (which stimulate gastric acid secretion), and following a liberalized bland diet omitting individual trigger foods and gastric irritants.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A (I, II, III and IV). All four interventions protect gastric mucosal integrity.

cards.front: The term that describes the volume of formula that remains in the stomach from a previous feeding is:
cards.rationale: Gastric Residual Volume (GRV) is the amount of unabsorbed enteral formula and secretions aspirated from the stomach via an enteral feeding tube before administering the next bolus or during continuous feeding to monitor gastric emptying and tolerance.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. gastric residual. Monitored in enteral nutrition support to prevent aspiration.

cards.front: What is the best nutritional assessment you as an ND utilize when diagnosing a food allergy?
cards.back: B. Have a patient keep a 1 week food/symptom record
options: A. Exclude foods with severe reactions only, but allow small quatities of foods with minor reactions
B. Have a patient keep a 1 week food/symptom record
C. Obtain a "reported" detailed food symptom record
D. Exclude foods causing a reaction
cards.rationale: A comprehensive prospective 1-to-2 week food and symptom diary recording exact foods, ingredients, cooking methods, quantities, timing of ingestion, and precise onset and nature of symptoms is the gold standard dietary assessment tool used by dietitians before structuring targeted elimination diets.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. Have a patient keep a 1 week food/symptom record. Diagnostic baseline for food allergies.

cards.front: What is the catabolic enzyme which can utilize peroxide in the production of substrates accompanied by water production?
cards.rationale: Catalase is a heme-containing antioxidant enzyme present in peroxisomes that catalyzes the decomposition of toxic hydrogen peroxide into water and molecular oxygen (2 H2O2 -> 2 H2O + O2), protecting cells against oxidative stress.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Catalase. Peroxisomal enzyme converting H2O2 to water and oxygen.

cards.front: Long-term management of diverticular disease includes a:
options: B. low-fiber diet that omits foods with seeds
cards.rationale: Long-term maintenance of diverticular disease (diverticulosis) requires a high-fiber diet (25 to 35 g/day or more) along with generous fluid intake to increase stool volume, soften feces, and decrease intraluminal colonic pressure, thereby preventing diverticulitis flares. Note that low fiber is only used during acute diverticulitis.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. high-fiber diet. Diverticulosis = High fiber; Diverticulitis (acute inflammation) = Low residue/low fiber or bowel rest.

cards.front: The cells that secrete the HCL in the body.
cards.rationale: Parietal (oxyntic) cells located in the gastric glands of the stomach fundus and corpus secrete hydrochloric acid (HCl) and intrinsic factor. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen; G-cells secrete the hormone gastrin.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. Parietal. Parietal = HCl + Intrinsic Factor; Chief = Pepsinogen; G-cells = Gastrin.

cards.front: Sudden hyperglycemia in a person who has consistently maintained good blood glucose control can be precipitated by _____.
options: B. conditions that lower levels of counter-regulatory hormones
cards.rationale: Acute infection, trauma, or systemic illness triggers a massive surge of stress and counter-regulatory hormones (epinephrine, cortisol, glucagon, growth hormone) and inflammatory cytokines. These hormones induce peripheral insulin resistance and stimulate hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, precipitating acute severe hyperglycemia.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. infection or illness. Infection induces counter-regulatory hormones causing acute glycemic spikes.

cards.front: The recommended fiber intake is _____ grams per day.
cards.rationale: Standard clinical nutrition guidelines (including the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and ADA) recommend a dietary fiber intake of 20 to 35 grams per day for healthy adults, or approximately 14 grams per 1,000 kcal.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. 20-35 grams per day. 14g/1000 kcal or 20-35 g/day is the standard board exam guideline.

cards.front: Which of the following describes water-soluble vitamins?
options: A. It includes vitamins C, D and E
C. It is stored extensively in the tissues.
cards.rationale: Water-soluble vitamins (B-complex vitamins and Vitamin C) are hydrophilic, dissolve freely in body fluids, are easily absorbed into the portal bloodstream, and excess amounts are readily excreted by the kidneys into urine. They have minimal tissue storage (except B12 in the liver) and rarely cause toxicity under physiological intakes.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. Easily absorbed and excreted. Water-soluble = B and C; excreted in urine; low toxicity risk.

cards.front: Nutrition support at the end of life should be carefully based on the following EXCEPT:
cards.rationale: In ethical clinical nutrition and palliative care, decisions regarding artificial nutrition support at the end of life must be centered primarily on patient autonomy (the patient's documented wishes or advance directives), overall prognosis, clinical burden vs. benefit, and palliative therapy goals. Family wishes cannot override competent patient wishes or clinical futility.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. family's wish. Medical ethics: Patient autonomy and clinical goals supersede third-party family demands.

cards.front: The body can make niacin from _____.
cards.rationale: The essential amino acid tryptophan serves as an endogenous precursor for nicotinic acid / nicotinamide (niacin). In human biochemistry, approximately 60 mg of dietary tryptophan can be converted into 1 mg of niacin equivalent (1 NE), a pathway requiring Vitamin B6 (PLP), riboflavin, and iron.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. tryptophan. 60 mg Tryptophan = 1 mg Niacin (1 NE).

cards.front: Sucrase, maltase and lactase are secreted by the _____.
cards.rationale: Disaccharidases—sucrase, maltase, and lactase—are brush-border enzymes embedded in the microvillar membrane of enterocytes in the small intestinal mucosa, where they hydrolyze disaccharides into monosaccharides for absorption.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. intestinal mucosa. Arrow drawn from gastric mucosa to intestinal mucosa.

cards.front: Absorption is the same as _____.
cards.rationale: Assimilation refers to the uptake and absorption of digested nutrient molecules across the intestinal mucosal barrier into the bloodstream or lymph, followed by their incorporation into living body cells and tissues.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. assimilation. Physiology definition: Absorption/assimilation is uptake into systemic circulation/cells.

cards.front: Diet recommendations for the nephrotic syndrome includes _____.
options: A. protein intakes that are less than the RENI
cards.rationale: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria, profound hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and severe edema. Sodium restriction (1 to 2 g/day, or 2 to 3 g salt) is essential to manage edema and hypertension. Dietary protein is maintained at normal levels (0.8–1.0 g/kg/day); high-protein intakes (>1.2 g/kg) are contraindicated because they accelerate glomerular hyperfiltration and worsen renal damage.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. sodium restrictions. Nephrotic syndrome: Normal protein (0.8-1.0 g/kg) + Sodium restriction for edema.

cards.front: Anti-cancer properties of phytochemicals include the following, EXCEPT;
cards.back: B. deactivation of detoxification system of the liver
options: B. deactivation of detoxification system of the liver
C. blocking of the metabolic pathway that can lead to carcinogenesis
cards.rationale: Phytochemicals (such as isothiocyanates, sulforaphane, indoles, and polyphenols) exert anti-cancer effects by INDUCING and activating Phase II hepatic detoxification enzymes, scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS), inhibiting tumor cell proliferation and angiogenesis, and inducing apoptosis. They do not deactivate hepatic detoxification systems.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. Phytochemicals induce/activate detoxification enzymes, not deactivate them.

cards.front: The diet principle that provides all the essential nutrients in sufficient amount to support health is _____.
cards.rationale: Dietary adequacy is the foundational diet-planning principle ensuring that a diet supplies sufficient energy and all essential nutrients to meet the physiological requirements of healthy individuals.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. adequacy. Adequacy = providing sufficient essential nutrients and energy.

cards.front: There are lots of variants to vegetarianism. The very strict variant is vegan while the least strict is _____.
cards.rationale: A semi-vegetarian (flexitarian) diet is the least restrictive vegetarian variant because it focuses primarily on plant-based foods while occasionally incorporating poultry, fish, seafood, dairy, and eggs. Veganism strictly excludes all animal products and byproducts.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. semi-vegetarian. Vegan = most strict; Semi-vegetarian/flexitarian = least strict.

cards.front: Increasing motivation through reinforcement is:
cards.back: C. Achieved by encouraging desirable behavior, while discouraging undesirable behavior
options: C. Achieved by encouraging desirable behavior, while discouraging undesirable behavior
D. only effective in producing short-term results
cards.rationale: In operant conditioning and behavioral counseling, reinforcement is used systematically to strengthen and maintain target healthy behaviors (positive reinforcement) while withholding reinforcement or applying corrective boundaries to extinguish maladaptive lifestyle habits.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Achieved by encouraging desirable behavior, while discouraging undesirable behavior.

cards.front: Dietary fibers are useful in preventing hypercholesterolemia because they:
cards.back: A. bind cholesterol containing bile acids which are eventually excreted
options: A. bind cholesterol containing bile acids which are eventually excreted
C. are carriers of omega-3 fatty acids
cards.rationale: Soluble viscous dietary fibers (pectin, beta-glucan, psyllium, gums) bind bile acids in the small intestine, interrupting enterohepatic circulation and causing bile acids to be excreted in feces. The liver is consequently forced to synthesize new bile acids from endogenous hepatic cholesterol pools, upregulating LDL receptors and lowering circulating serum cholesterol.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. bind cholesterol containing bile acids which are eventually excreted.

cards.front: Which of these fruits is a good source of Vitamin A?
cards.rationale: Papaya is an excellent tropical fruit source of provitamin A carotenoids (notably beta-carotene and beta-cryptoxanthin), which are enzymatically cleaved into retinal and retinol in enterocytes.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: Papaya (Option B/C depending on labeling). Papaya is rich in beta-carotene.

cards.front: Which theory of counseling did you use in the following scenario: You were asked to counsel a single-parent of a two-year old due to excessive temper tantrums at meal-times. Determine which model theory for healthy eating behavior at meal-times and sharing parenting tips of this age group would be beneficial?
cards.rationale: Albert Bandura's Social Learning Theory (Social Cognitive Theory) emphasizes that behaviors are acquired and modified through observational learning, modeling, reciprocal determinism, and social interactions. In pediatric feeding counseling, parental role-modeling and shared peer-group learning reinforce healthy mealtime behaviors.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. Social Learning Theory. Bandura's theory emphasizes modeling and observational learning.

cards.front: Mouth sores in people with HIV infection are most frequently due to:
cards.rationale: Due to impaired cell-mediated immunity (CD4+ T-lymphocyte depletion), patients with HIV/AIDS frequently suffer from opportunistic oral infections, most commonly oral candidiasis (thrush, Candida albicans), herpes simplex virus (HSV) stomatitis, oral hairy leukoplakia, and aphthous ulcers.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. oral infections. Opportunistic candidiasis and HSV stomatitis cause HIV mouth sores.

cards.front: An obese child client is on your Weight Loss Program. After the initial interview, you found out that she doesn't eat vegetables and fruits, is fond of processed foods, loves cakes and ice cream. Establishing rapport is the first thing you do. Mention the award/reward will be given to encourage the child to cooperate. Which theory of counseling is used in this kind of scenario?
cards.rationale: Using contingency management, positive incentives, and reward systems to motivate and reinforce dietary compliance and lifestyle modifications in children falls under rewards compensation / reinforcement theory.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. Rewards Compensation Theory. Operant conditioning utilizing external rewards for compliance.

cards.front: Essential fatty acids includes:
cards.rationale: Linoleic acid (18:2 n-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (18:3 n-3) are the two true essential fatty acids in human nutrition because mammalian cells lack delta-12 and delta-15 desaturase enzymes required to introduce double bonds beyond carbon 9 from the carboxyl terminal.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. Linoleic and linolenic acid. Essential fatty acids: Omega-6 (Linoleic) and Omega-3 (Alpha-linolenic).

cards.front: Choose an accurate non-invasive test seen in dehydrated patients.
cards.rationale: Urine color assessment (using validated urine color charts) is an immediate, accurate, bedside non-invasive indicator of hydration status. Dark, concentrated amber urine reflects elevated urine specific gravity and osmolality caused by maximal renal water reabsorption under ADH stimulation in dehydration.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. Dark colored urine. Non-invasive clinical physical sign of volume depletion.

cards.front: JM is a 10 years old boy, diagnosed with Nephrotic Syndrome. His laboratory test results show that his sodium level is low, and his potassium level is borderline. What is the primary manifestation of Nephrotic Syndrome?
cards.rationale: The primary and initiating pathophysiological hallmark of Nephrotic Syndrome is heavy glomerular proteinuria (>3.5 g/24 hr in adults or >40 mg/m2/hr in children) caused by loss of glomerular podocyte charge and size selectivity. This massive protein leak triggers hypoalbuminemia, decreased oncotic pressure, and third-spacing edema.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. Proteinuria (and C. Edema highlighted). Primary initiating lesion is proteinuria.

cards.front: Vitamins whose requirements are dependent on a person's energy intake.
cards.rationale: Thiamin (B1), Riboflavin (B2), and Niacin (B3) serve as indispensable coenzymes in cellular energy metabolism (TPP, FMN/FAD, and NAD/NADP in glycolysis, Krebs cycle, and electron transport chain). Their recommended daily allowances are directly calculated per 1,000 kcal of total energy intake.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Thiamin and Riboflavin. B1, B2, and B3 coenzymes scale directly with total caloric expenditure.

cards.front: Which of the following is NOT a component of bile?
cards.rationale: Hepatic bile consists primarily of bile salts (conjugated bile acids), phospholipids (principally phosphatidylcholine/lecithin), cholesterol, and bile pigments (bilirubin glucuronide). Sodium bicarbonate is predominantly secreted by pancreatic ductal cells in response to secretin to neutralize acidic gastric chyme in the duodenum, not a major constituent of gallbladder bile.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. Sodium bicarbonate. Bile = bile acids, cholesterol, lecithin, bilirubin. Bicarbonate = pancreatic juice.

cards.front: Digestion and absorption are coordinated by the _____.
cards.rationale: Gastrointestinal motility, secretomotor functions, and absorptive capacities are coordinated via neuroendocrine feedback mechanisms: the enteric and autonomic nervous systems (vagal parasympathetic and sympathetic innervation) and peptide gastrointestinal hormones (gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin, GIP, GLP-1).
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. hormonal and nervous system. Gut-brain axis and neuroendocrine regulation.

cards.front: What is function of the pyloric sphincter?
cards.back: C. Regulates the flow of partially digested food into the small intestine
options: A. Holds food in the stomach long enough for it to be liquified
B. Prevents the small intestines from backing up to the stomach
C. Regulates the flow of partially digested food into the small intestine
D. Holds food in the stomach long enough for it to be liquified
cards.rationale: The pyloric sphincter is the smooth muscle band separating the gastric pylorus from the duodenal bulb that acts as a dynamic valve, regulating and metering the rate at which acidic, partially digested chyme empties into the duodenum.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Regulates the flow of partially digested food into the small intestine.

cards.front: Diverticulosis is a condition associated with:
cards.rationale: Chronic low-fiber intake results in small-caliber, hard stools that require high segmental intracolonic pressures to propel during peristalsis. Over decades, this excessive pressure herniates colonic mucosa through weakened areas of the muscular circular layer, forming diverticula.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. low-fiber diet. Etiology of diverticulosis: chronic low-fiber intake causing high intracolonic pressure.

cards.front: What is the energy producer of the cell?
cards.rationale: Mitochondria are the powerhouses of eukaryotic cells, housing the citric acid cycle (TCA cycle), fatty acid beta-oxidation, and the electron transport chain coupled with ATP synthase for oxidative phosphorylation.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Mitochondria. Site of oxidative phosphorylation and cellular ATP production.

cards.front: What is a primary concern a clinical dietitian has when managing oncology patient?
cards.rationale: Cancer-related malnutrition and cancer anorexia-cachexia syndrome affect up to 80% of oncology patients and directly impair tolerance to chemotherapy and radiation, increase postoperative complications, degrade functional performance, and contribute directly to mortality.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Malnutrition. Primary MNT target in oncology: preventing and managing cancer-induced malnutrition/cachexia.

cards.front: The fluid mixed with the patients blood during dialysis is called:
cards.rationale: Dialysate is the sterile aqueous fluid containing balanced electrolytes (sodium, bicarbonate, calcium, potassium) and glucose that flows through the dialyzer counter-current to blood to facilitate solute diffusion and fluid ultrafiltration. (The dialyzer is the artificial kidney cartridge).
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. dialyzate. Dialyzer = artificial filter machine; Dialysate = fluid solution.

cards.front: Which of the following symptom is Respiratory?
cards.rationale: Wheezing (bronchospasm), sneezing (rhinitis), and airway congestion are classical respiratory signs and symptoms resulting from mucosal inflammation, allergic hypersensitivity, or respiratory disease.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. wheezing, sneezing, congestion. Classic respiratory signs in allergy assessment.

cards.front:
Which of these should be monitored regularly among patients on dialysis?
I. Weight
II. Blood pressure
III. Urine output
IV. Body fat
options: D. I, II, III and IV
cards.rationale: Dialysis patients must monitor dry weight daily (to track interdialytic fluid weight gain), blood pressure (to identify hypertension from fluid overload or hypotension from rapid ultrafiltration), and residual urine output (to adjust fluid allowances). Routine body fat percentage is not measured on a frequent/daily basis.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C (I, II and III). Key monitoring parameters in hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis.

cards.front: The glycerol portion of fat is used by the liver for _____.
cards.rationale: Glycerol released from lipolysis is phosphorylated by hepatic glycerol kinase to glycerol-3-phosphate, which serves as the direct carbohydrate backbone for triglyceride synthesis (re-esterification) or is oxidized to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) for glycolysis or gluconeogenesis.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. triglyceride synthesis. Glycerol-3-phosphate is re-esterified into triglycerides in hepatocytes.

cards.front: All nutrients needed by the body follows this statement.
cards.back: C. Are supplied by a variety of foods in many different combinations.
options: A. Have a variety of functions and uses in the body.
B. Must follow specific food combinations.
C. Are supplied by a variety of foods in many different combinations.
D. It must be obtained through vitamin and mineral supplementation
cards.rationale: A central tenet of human nutrition is that no single natural food supplies all essential nutrients in optimal quantities; a diverse variety of foods from different food groups consumed in varied combinations is required to achieve complete nutritional adequacy.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Are supplied by a variety of foods in many different combinations.

cards.front: Two factors that contribute to the maintenance of basal metabolic rate are:
cards.rationale: Basal metabolic rate (BMR) represents the obligatory energetic cost of sustaining basic vegetative life at complete physical and emotional rest, which includes involuntary cardiac muscle contraction (heartbeat), respiratory work, brain cellular metabolism, and maintenance of core body temperature.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. heartbeat and body temperature. Involuntary vegetative metabolic demands.

cards.front: The need for Vit. B1 increases in the following conditions, EXCEPT
cards.rationale: Thiamin pyrophosphate (TPP) is an essential coenzyme for enzymes of carbohydrate metabolism (pyruvate dehydrogenase, transketolase). Increased carbohydrate/calorie intake, pregnancy, and alcohol use elevate thiamin requirements. Conversely, fats have a 'thiamin-sparing effect' because fatty acid beta-oxidation does not require TPP, so increased fat consumption does not increase thiamin needs.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Increase fat consumption. Fat metabolism spares thiamin; high carb intake increases B1 demand.

cards.front: Lily was diagnosed with hyperkalemia. Which of the following statements will you use to explain to Lily the bad affects of high serum potassium level?
cards.back: C. This can cause cardiac arrest and may be fatal
options: A. It will lead to arthritis
B. Antagonists action of calcium and causes bone demineralization
C. This can cause cardiac arrest and may be fatal
D. It will induce extreme thirst
cards.rationale: Severe hyperkalemia (serum potassium > 6.0–6.5 mEq/L) causes partial depolarization of the cardiac muscle cell membrane resting potential, leading to peaked T waves, conduction blocks, ventricular fibrillation, and fatal diastolic cardiac arrest.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. This can cause cardiac arrest and may be fatal. Critical electrolyte toxicity in clinical practice.

cards.front: Why is it important to regulate the release of chyme into the duodenum?
cards.back: D. Duodenum is small and cannot accommodate too much chyme.
options: A. Only small amounts of juice can be secreted to digest chyme.
B. Stomach needs to have chyme all the time.
C. Small intestine has limited mucous coating to protect from acids.
D. Duodenum is small and cannot accommodate too much chyme.
cards.rationale: Controlled gastric emptying through the pyloric sphincter is essential because the duodenum has a limited intraluminal volume and buffering capacity. Rapid entry of hypertonic, acidic gastric chyme causes duodenal distension, fluid shifts, cramping, and vasomotor dumping syndrome.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. Duodenum is small and cannot accommodate too much chyme. (Option C also notes acid vulnerability).

cards.front: Organs that detoxifies alcohol. Other drugs and poisons, prepares waste products for excretion.
cards.rationale: The liver is the principal metabolic and detoxifying organ of the body. Hepatocytes express alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH), aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH), and the microsomal ethanol oxidizing system (CYP2E1) to metabolize ethanol, as well as Phase I and Phase II cytochrome P450 enzyme complexes to neutralize xenobiotics, drugs, and poisons for biliary or urinary elimination.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. Liver. Primary site of drug biotransformation and alcohol oxidation.

cards.front: What is the maximum amount of alcohol a man with diabetes can take per day?
cards.rationale: According to the American Diabetes Association (ADA) and clinical nutrition guidelines, if adult patients with diabetes choose to drink alcohol, intake should be limited to a maximum of 2 standard drinks per day for men and 1 standard drink per day for women, always consumed with food to prevent delayed nocturnal hypoglycemia.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. 2 drinks (exam paper had duplicate choices: A. 2 drinks, B. 1 drinks; D was marked 1 drink, corrected to A. 2 drinks for men).

cards.front: Vitamin E acts as a _____ of free radicals.
cards.rationale: Alpha-tocopherol (Vitamin E) is a lipid-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant that functions as a scavenger of free radicals (specifically peroxyl radicals), intercepting lipid peroxidation chain reactions in cellular membranes and circulating lipoproteins.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. scavenger. Lipophilic antioxidant chain-breaking scavenger.

cards.front: Major organ where intermediary metabolism takes place.
cards.rationale: The liver is the central clearinghouse and master organ of intermediary metabolism, carrying out glycogenesis, glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, ketogenesis, transamination, deamination, and the urea cycle.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Liver. Metabolic hub for carbohydrate, lipid, and protein intermediary pathways.

cards.front: re counseling a person with Type 1 Diabetes who intends to do regular exercise. Which of the following advise should you EMPHASIZE?
cards.back: D. Monitor if possible, blood glucose before, during and after exercise.
options: A. He must know the symptoms of hypoglycemia for precautionary measure.
B. Take additional carbohydrate as snack before exercise.
D. Monitor if possible, blood glucose before, during and after exercise.
cards.rationale: For individuals with Type 1 Diabetes engaging in physical activity, self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) before, during, and after exercise is the most critical foundation. It provides the empirical data necessary to detect impending exercise-induced hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, allowing precise carbohydrate supplementation and insulin dosage adjustments.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. Monitor if possible, blood glucose before, during and after exercise.

cards.front: Diet therapy for people with delayed gastric emptying most often includes;
options: D. high fiber foods given in frequent small meals
cards.rationale: In gastroparesis (delayed gastric emptying), dietary fat is restricted because it stimulates cholecystokinin (CCK) secretion, which physiologically inhibits gastric motility. Dietary fiber (especially viscous/insoluble fibers) is restricted to avoid delayed emptying and reduce the risk of phytobezoar formation. Meals should also be small, frequent, and semi-liquid or puréed.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. low-fiber, low fat foods. Gastroparesis MNT: Low fat + low fiber + frequent small meals.

cards.front: Which of these water-soluble vitamins will increase with energy intake?
cards.rationale: Niacin (along with thiamin and riboflavin) functions directly as an electron carrier (NAD+/NADH and NADP+/NADPH) across all fuel catabolic pathways. Because higher caloric intake demands greater flux through glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation, niacin requirements scale directly with total caloric expenditure.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Niacin. B1, B2, and B3 requirements correlate directly with energy intake.

cards.front: It is an examination and a fundamental component of nutrition assessment that will show signs of malnutrition, can test grip strength to assess physical function. Hands on training is required.
cards.rationale: The Nutrition Focused Physical Examination (NFPE) is a systematic head-to-toe clinical assessment conducted by registered nutritionist-dietitians to identify physical signs of malnutrition, subcutaneous fat loss, muscle mass wasting, fluid accumulation (edema/ascites), micronutrient deficiencies, and functional status via handgrip dynamometry.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Nutrition Focused Physical Examination (NFPE). Hands-on physical and functional assessment.

cards.front: A 10 year-old boy weighs 120 lbs, 5 ft tall, BMI = 23, placing him above the 95th percentile for weight-for-age, so he is _____.
cards.rationale: According to pediatric growth charts, a child with BMI >= 95th percentile for age and sex is classified as obese (or overweight/obese in older terminology). Between the 85th and <95th percentile is overweight, and <5th percentile is underweight. In the PRC exam key, choice C (overweight) is designated.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. overweight. BMI >= 95th percentile in pediatrics denotes obesity/overweight.

cards.front: Which of the following medical nutritionals contains partially digested?
cards.rationale: Elemental (monomeric) and semi-elemental (oligomeric/peptide-based) enteral medical nutritional formulas contain predigested or partially digested macronutrients—specifically free amino acids or small peptides, simple carbohydrates, and minimal fats (MCTs)—designed for patients with compromised digestive or absorptive capacity.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. amino acids. Elemental formulas feature free amino acids/peptides.

cards.front: Which of the following is NOT a clinical consequence of refeeding syndrome?
cards.rationale: The hallmark biochemical derangements of refeeding syndrome are acute, severe intracellular electrolyte shifts causing profound HYPOphosphatemia, HYPOkalemia, and HYPOmagnesemia. While sodium and fluid retention occur due to insulin's antinatriuretic action on renal tubules, 'hypervolemia' is not the signature defining intracellular electrolyte depletion.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. hypervolemia. Hallmark triad of refeeding syndrome: Hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia.

cards.front:
Exchange choices for 2 oz. meat
I. 2 oz fish fillet
II. 1 cup mongo
III. 2 oz. chicken
IV. 1 glass milk
options: A. I, II, III and IV
cards.rationale: In the Philippine Food Exchange Lists (PEL), 1 meat exchange is equivalent to 1 oz (30 grams) of cooked meat, poultry, or fish. Therefore, 2 oz of fish fillet (I) and 2 oz of chicken (III) each provide exactly 2 meat exchanges. Cooked mongo is classified under legumes/vegetables, and milk is classified under the milk exchange list.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. I and III. 1 meat exchange = 1 oz cooked meat/fish (8g PRO, 1-7g FAT).

cards.front: Adverse food and drug interactions are more likely to occur if:
cards.back: D. the person taking the medication is malnourished
options: A. all organ systems are fully functional
B. one medication or herb is taken exclusively
C. medications and dietary supplements are taken for a few days
D. the person taking the medication is malnourished
cards.rationale: Malnutrition causes hypoalbuminemia, which reduces plasma protein-binding capacity for highly bound acidic drugs, resulting in higher circulating fractions of free active drug and potential toxicity. Furthermore, severe malnutrition impairs hepatic cytochrome P450 drug-metabolizing enzymes and renal excretion.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. the person taking the medication is malnourished. Hypoalbuminemia increases free pharmacologically active drug levels.

cards.front: With the ND Law of 2016, the mandate is for the profession to go into Accredited Integrated Profession Organization. As mandated, the AIPO should qualify in the requirements EXCEPT:
cards.back: B. members may be less in number than the other ND organization provided, it has members who can lead the organization to greater heights through alignment with international practices
options: A. it will be the umbrella organization of the other associations that have RNDs as members
B. members may be less in number than the other ND organization provided, it has members who can lead the organization to greater heights through alignment with international practices
C. new CBL that will address the updated requirement of PRC
D. professional organization should be composed of RND members only
cards.rationale: Under Republic Act No. 10862 (Nutrition and Dietetics Law of 2016) and PRC regulations, the designated Accredited Integrated Professional Organization (AIPO, such as NDAP) must represent the largest single registered membership of RNDs across the country. It cannot have fewer members than other rival organizations.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. RA 10862 requires the AIPO to represent the national majority of registered practitioners.

cards.front: An important Vitamin that is also considered a hormone. To help prescribe the right dose for supplementation, it is important to request for a quantitative test.
cards.rationale: Vitamin D is synthesized endogenously in the skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol via ultraviolet B sunlight and converted to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), which acts through nuclear receptors to regulate gene transcription. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] is the standard quantitative laboratory biomarker used to assess status and dose therapeutic supplementation.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. Vitamin D. Calcitriol acts as a secosteroid hormone; measured via serum 25(OH)D.

cards.front: A diet principle that refers to consuming different foods from within each of the food groups on a regular basis.
cards.rationale: Variety (or diversity) refers to choosing a wide array of different foods both between and within each of the basic food groups on a regular basis, which ensures intake of diverse nutrients and non-nutrient bioactive phytochemicals.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. Variety. Consuming different foods within each food group.

cards.front: The Prochaska Cycle of change where a person would sustain change occurs is:
cards.rationale: In Prochaska and DiClemente's Transtheoretical Model (Stages of Change), the Maintenance stage is defined as sustaining the newly adopted behavior and lifestyle modifications for six months or longer, actively working to prevent relapse.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Maintenance. Transtheoretical Model: Sustaining behavior change >= 6 months.

cards.front: Herbs and spices:
cards.back: B. may be used in sodium restricted diet
options: A. should be avoided in sodium restricted diet
B. may be used in sodium restricted diet
C. may increase sodium content of the food
D. should be used only in mild sodium restricted diet
cards.rationale: Pure natural culinary herbs and spices (such as garlic, basil, oregano, thyme, cinnamon, cumin, and black pepper) are naturally very low in sodium. They are strongly recommended in sodium-restricted diets to enhance aroma and flavor, compensating for reduced salt and improving diet adherence.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. may be used in sodium restricted diet. Safe natural seasonings for hypertension and CHF.

cards.front: Which strategy is safe for increasing the energy intake of people on fat-restricted diets?
cards.back: B. Provide additional fat in the form of MCT oil or MCT powder
options: A. Gradually add fat as tolerance permits
B. Provide additional fat in the form of MCT oil or MCT powder
D. Provide fat with enzyme replacement
cards.rationale: For patients with fat malabsorption (such as in chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, or biliary obstruction), Medium-Chain Triglycerides (MCT oil or powder) provide 8.3 kcal/g and are absorbed directly into enterocytes without requiring bile salt micellization or pancreatic lipase digestion, avoiding steatorrhea.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B / D (Exam duplicate of Q5). MCT oil is the safe caloric supplement in fat restriction.

cards.front: Your client is a marathon runner. Your advice will focus on how to decrease the risk of exercise-related GI problems which is to _____.
cards.back: D. avoid dairy products prior to exercise
options: A. consume high fructose beverage an hour prior, to enhance blood glucose levels
B. avoid fluids before and during exercise to avoid cramps
C. consume high-fiber foods an hour prior to exercise to slow CHO absorption and maximize blood glucose during exercise
D. avoid dairy products prior to exercise
cards.rationale: Exercise-related gastrointestinal distress ('runner's gut', ischemia, bloating, diarrhea) is frequently exacerbated by lactose (found in dairy), concentrated fructose solutions, insoluble fiber, and high-fat foods consumed prior to endurance events. Eliminating dairy products and low-lactose alternatives prior to running prevents osmotic shifts and cramping.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. avoid dairy products prior to exercise. Dairy/lactose before endurance running triggers GI cramping.

cards.front: Which of this is NOT needed to digest protein?
cards.rationale: Bile acids are amphipathic molecules synthesized in the liver that emulsify dietary lipids and form mixed micelles for fat absorption; they have no direct enzymatic or catalytic function in protein digestion. Trypsin, pepsin (activated by HCl), and secretin (which stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate to create an alkaline pH for pancreatic endopeptidases) are all involved in protein digestion.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. Bile acid. Bile acids emulsify lipids, playing no enzymatic role in proteolysis.

cards.front: After an ileostomy, the most serious concern is that:
cards.back: D. incompletely digested foods may cause obstruction
options: A. the diet is so restrictive to meet nutrient needs
B. fluid restriction prevents patients from drinking beverage freely
C. water disposal causes frequent daily interruption
D. incompletely digested foods may cause obstruction
cards.rationale: Because an ileostomy bypasses the colon and terminates in a narrow stoma on the abdominal wall, poorly chewed, stringy, or fibrous foods (such as celery, corn kernels, popcorn, nuts, seeds, coconut, tough meat fibers) can easily lodge in the narrow lumen of the stoma, causing a mechanical bowel obstruction.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. incompletely digested foods may cause obstruction. High-fiber/stringy foods risk stomal obstruction.

cards.front: Two activities that contribute to the basal metabolic rate are:
cards.back: A. Maintenance of heartbeat and body temperature
options: A. Maintenance of heartbeat and body temperature
B. Maintenance of body temperature and walking
D. Maintenance of heartbeat and running
cards.rationale: Basal metabolic rate (BMR) measures energy expenditure at rest in a post-absorptive, thermoneutral state. Heart contraction (circulatory work) and core thermoregulation are two classic autonomic physiological components sustaining BMR.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. Maintenance of heartbeat and body temperature.

cards.front: If your patient is breathing rapidly, his body is attempting to:
cards.back: B. get rid of excess CO2
options: B. get rid of excess CO2
D. improve the buffering ability of the bicarbonate
cards.rationale: Rapid, deep respirations (tachypnea or Kussmaul respirations) represent respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis. By hyperventilating, the lungs blow off volatile carbon dioxide (CO2), driving the carbonic acid reaction to the left (H+ + HCO3- <-> H2CO3 <-> CO2 + H2O), thereby lowering hydrogen ion concentration and raising arterial blood pH.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. get rid of excess CO2. Hyperventilation blows off CO2 to correct acidosis.

cards.front: Who is most at risk for gestational diabetes?
cards.back: D. BMI > 30 with history of GDM
options: B. Conception within 10 months of last pregnancy
C. Age younger than 25 but overweight
D. BMI > 30 with history of GDM
cards.rationale: Pre-gravid obesity (BMI > 30 kg/m2) coupled with a personal history of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) represents the single greatest risk profile for developing GDM in subsequent pregnancies due to underlying peripheral insulin resistance.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. BMI > 30 with history of GDM. Major established risk factors for GDM.

cards.front: Nutrient that is MOST commonly malabsorbed.
cards.rationale: Lipid (fat) digestion and absorption is the most physiologically complex digestive process, requiring gastric lipase, biliary emulsification, pancreatic lipase-colipase, mixed micelle formation, mucosal re-esterification, and lymphatic chylomicron assembly. Consequently, gastrointestinal disorders (pancreatitis, liver cirrhosis, mucosal atrophy, mucosal resections) most readily manifest as fat malabsorption (steatorrhea).
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. Lipids. Fat is the most vulnerable and commonly malabsorbed macronutrient.

cards.front: Which statements BEST describes the dialysis process?
cards.back: C. The diffusion of blood across a semipermeable membrane which is then cleansed.
options: A. The filtering of toxicities in the urine.
B. The removal of urine in the bladder.
C. The diffusion of blood across a semipermeable membrane which is then cleansed.
D. The removal of toxicities in the human body.
cards.rationale: Dialysis is an extracorporeal renal replacement therapy based on the biophysical principles of diffusion (solute movement down a concentration gradient across a semipermeable membrane) and ultrafiltration (fluid movement across a pressure gradient), cleansing the blood of uremic toxins and excess fluid.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. The diffusion of blood across a semipermeable membrane which is then cleansed.

cards.front: Trauma a deeply distressing experience can place a patient in a/an _____ state.
cards.rationale: Major physical trauma, burns, and severe critical illness trigger an acute neuroendocrine stress response (flow phase) mediated by catecholamines, cortisol, glucagon, and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha), resulting in marked hypermetabolism, accelerated proteolysis, and negative nitrogen balance.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. hypermetabolic. Metabolic stress flow phase: hypermetabolism and hypercatabolism.

cards.front: It is the rate and the extent to which a vitamin is absorbed and use in the body.
cards.rationale: Bioavailability is defined in nutritional biochemistry and pharmacology as the proportion of an ingested nutrient or active compound that is digested, absorbed across the gastrointestinal tract, and reaches systemic circulation to be utilized for physiological functions.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. Bioavailability. Definition of nutrient bioavailability.

cards.front: A common disorder characterized by a disturbance the motility of the GI tract with symptoms that frequently occur shortly after a person eats is called:
cards.rationale: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder of the brain-gut axis characterized by visceral hypersensitivity, altered gut motility, and recurrent abdominal pain or bloating frequently exacerbated postprandially (after eating).
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. irritable bowel syndrome. Functional motility disorder with postprandial exacerbations.

cards.front: When you make a teaching plan for your counseling session, which of the following will create a learning situation that will secure attention and interest. Stimulate learning readiness.
cards.rationale: In instructional design and health education planning, the 'Approach' (or anticipatory set/introduction) is designed specifically to capture the client's attention, pique personal curiosity, relate new material to prior experiences, and stimulate psychological readiness to learn.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. Approach (D. Application was also circled, but B represents engaging readiness/attention).

cards.front: A serious primary problem resulting from prolonged vomiting from chemotherapy relates to:
cards.rationale: Prolonged emesis leads to massive loss of gastric hydrochloric acid, water, potassium, and sodium. The immediate life-threatening physiological complications are dehydration, hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis, disrupting fluid and electrolyte homeostasis.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. fluid and electrolyte balance. Emesis causes severe volume depletion and hypokalemic alkalosis.

cards.front:
Cancer primary treatment goals for nutrition intervention include:
I. Preventing or reversing nutrient deficiencies
II. Preserving lean body mass
III. Minimizing and managing nutrition impact symptoms and side effects
IV. Maximizing quality of life
cards.rationale: According to ESPEN and ASPEN oncology nutrition guidelines, comprehensive MNT goals for cancer patients encompass: (I) preventing and reversing nutrient deficiencies, (II) preserving skeletal muscle and lean body mass, (III) minimizing nutrition impact symptoms (nausea, mucositis, dysgeusia), and (IV) maintaining functional status and quality of life.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B (I, II, III & IV). All 4 are core oncology nutrition goals.

cards.front: Mary had a poor appetite for several days. Strategies that may be used to improve your client's food intake may include any of the following EXCEPT;
cards.back: D. feed the client by tube
options: A. assist the client during meals
B. serve food that are easy to eat
C. provide energy and nutrient-dense foods
D. feed the client by tube
cards.rationale: Initial dietary strategies to stimulate and improve oral food intake in anorexia include: meal assistance, serving palatable and easy-to-chew foods, small frequent energy-dense meals, and oral nutritional supplements. Tube feeding is an invasive enteral therapy indicated only when voluntary oral intake remains inadequate (<50-60%) over prolonged periods, not an oral intake strategy.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. feed the client by tube. Tube feeding is invasive enteral support, not an oral strategy.

cards.front: Which is NOT part of the clinical RNDs task?
cards.rationale: Clinical Registered Nutritionist-Dietitians (RNDs) are responsible for individual patient clinical care: nutritional assessment, NCP diagnosis, nutrition intervention, medical record charting (ADIME format), and inpatient/discharge nutrition counseling. Large-scale institutional food service menu planning is an administrative/food service management task.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. Food service menu planning. Clinical RND focuses on patient-centered care and NCP.

cards.front: Azotemia is detected through the measurement of _____.
options: A. Sodium in the spinal fluid
cards.rationale: Azotemia is an abnormal clinical and biochemical elevation of nitrogenous waste products in the blood, primarily diagnosed and monitored by measuring Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) and serum creatinine.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. Blood urea nitrogen. Azotemia = elevated BUN and nitrogenous wastes.

cards.front: The middle segment of the small intestine?
cards.rationale: Anatomically, the small intestine comprises three contiguous segments: the duodenum (first/proximal, ~25 cm), the jejunum (middle, ~2.5 m), and the ileum (distal, ~3.5 m).
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. Jejunum. Small bowel order: Duodenum -> Jejunum -> Ileum.

cards.front: Your patient are doing discharge counseling with respiratory failure, your instruction should be to limit his intake of;
cards.rationale: In respiratory failure and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), carbohydrate oxidation yields a Respiratory Quotient (RQ) of 1.0 (RQ = VCO2 / VO2), producing significantly more carbon dioxide per mole of oxygen consumed than fat oxidation (RQ = 0.7). Excess dietary carbohydrates increase ventilatory demand and CO2 retention, exacerbating hypercapnic respiratory failure.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. Carbohydrates. High CHO increases CO2 production (RQ = 1.0).

cards.front: The primary goal of medical nutrition therapy in diabetes is to _____.
cards.back: C. maintain near-normal blood glucose levels
options: B. control blood lipids and blood pressure
C. maintain near-normal blood glucose levels
cards.rationale: While cardiovascular risk reduction and weight management are vital components of comprehensive diabetes management, the primary and central therapeutic goal of MNT in diabetes is to achieve and maintain near-normal blood glucose levels (glycemic control, HbA1c < 7.0%) to prevent acute ketoacidosis/hypoglycemia and long-term microvascular and macrovascular complications.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. maintain near-normal blood glucose levels. Primary glycemic objective in diabetes MNT.

cards.front: The patient with chronic pancreatitis benefits from the following diet-related advice:
cards.back: A. use enzyme replacements to improve fat absorption
options: A. use enzyme replacements to improve fat absorption
B. follow a very low fat diet
C. eat three meals a day and avoid snacks
cards.rationale: Chronic pancreatitis leads to progressive loss of pancreatic exocrine tissue, causing lipase deficiency and severe steatorrhea. Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT) taken concurrently with all meals and snacks restores lipid digestion, improves nutrient absorption, and relieves abdominal pain and diarrhea. Note: Alcohol must be strictly eliminated, not moderately restricted.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. use enzyme replacements to improve fat absorption. PERT is the cornerstone of chronic pancreatitis MNT.

cards.front: Which are the symptoms of respiratory problem?
options: D. Swollen throat, bloating and malabsorption
cards.rationale: Wheezing (bronchial narrowing/spasm), sneezing (upper airway rhinitis), and respiratory congestion are hallmark clinical manifestations of respiratory illness or respiratory-involved systemic allergic reactions.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Wheezing, sneezing and congestion. Respiratory clinical symptoms.

cards.front: Which of the following represents a potential affect of infection on nutritional status?
cards.rationale: Systemic infection stimulates inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha) and glucocorticoids, accelerating skeletal muscle proteolysis (protein catabolism) to mobilize amino acids for hepatic acute-phase protein synthesis and gluconeogenesis, producing negative nitrogen balance.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. Protein catabolism. Infection triggers cytokine-mediated muscle catabolism.

cards.front: For the person undergoing a liver transplant:
cards.back: B. attention to nutrients before a transplant improves chances of recovery
options: A. enteral nutrition is contraindicated following the transplant
B. attention to nutrients before a transplant improves chances of recovery
C. provided adequate nutrition is given following a transplant, nutrition status before surgery has little impact on recovery
D. immunosuppressant drugs seldom alter nutrient needs
cards.rationale: Malnutrition is present in up to 80-90% of end-stage liver disease patients awaiting transplantation and is an independent predictor of operative morbidity, prolonged mechanical ventilation, sepsis, and post-transplant mortality. Pre-transplant nutrition intervention significantly enhances graft survival and surgical recovery.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. attention to nutrients before a transplant improves chances of recovery.

cards.front: Ammonia is detoxified when the liver converts it to _____.
cards.rationale: Free neurotoxic ammonia (NH3/NH4+) produced by amino acid deamination and colonic bacterial ureases is transported to the liver, where hepatocytes convert it into non-toxic, water-soluble urea via the hepatic urea cycle (ornithine cycle) for ultimate renal clearance.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. urea. Hepatic urea cycle detoxifies ammonia to urea.

cards.front: Which of the following results fall within the normal blood glucose levels?
cards.rationale: According to the American Diabetes Association (ADA) diagnostic guidelines, normal fasting plasma glucose is defined as 70 to 99 mg/dL (or 70 to 100 mg/dL). Fasting glucose from 100 to 125 mg/dL is categorized as impaired fasting glucose (prediabetes), and >= 126 mg/dL indicates diabetes mellitus.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. 70 - 100 mg/dL. Standard clinical normal fasting plasma glucose range.

cards.front: Ammonia is detoxified when the liver converts it to:
cards.rationale: Free ammonia is metabolized exclusively via the hepatic ornithine-urea cycle into neutral, water-soluble urea, which enters systemic circulation and is filtered by renal glomeruli.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. Urea (Exam paper duplicate of Q94).

cards.front: When renal tissue has been destroyed to a point at which it can no longer filter the blood, the following occurs _____.
cards.rationale: When end-stage renal disease (ESRD) develops and the glomerular filtration rate falls profoundly, kidneys can no longer clear nitrogenous wastes, electrolytes, and water. This profound intoxication of tissues and organs by accumulated nitrogenous waste products is termed uremia (uremic syndrome).
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. Uremia. End-stage toxemia due to loss of renal excretory function.

cards.front: Which of the following uses advance scientific techniques to alter and ideally improve characteristics of plants, animals and other forms of life?
cards.rationale: Biotechnology is the broad, encompassing scientific discipline that applies cellular and biomolecular processes (including recombinant DNA technology, genetic modification, and cloning) to improve agricultural crops, food crops, and medicinal organisms.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Biotechnology. Broad umbrella term for molecular biological alteration.

cards.front: Which type of fiber binds bile and therefore reduces one's risk of atherosclerosis?
cards.rationale: Soluble viscous fiber (such as beta-glucan from oats, pectin from citrus fruits, and psyllium) forms viscous gels in the intestinal lumen that bind bile acids and dietary cholesterol, preventing micellar reabsorption and stimulating hepatic conversion of cholesterol into bile acids, reducing serum atherogenic LDL cholesterol.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Soluble fiber. Soluble fiber binds bile acids to lower LDL and cardiovascular risk.

cards.front:
Using the PEL as basis, approximately how many grams of protein will this meal provide?
- 3/4 cup rice
- 3 exchanges of fried chicken breast
- 1 cup salad greens with vinegar as dressing
- 1 exchange banana
cards.rationale:
Calculation using the Philippine Food Exchange Lists (PEL):
1. Rice: 1 exchange = 1/2 cup cooked rice = 2 g protein. Thus, 3/4 cup cooked rice = 1.5 exchanges * 2 g = 3 g protein.
2. Chicken breast: 1 exchange of lean/medium meat = 8 g protein. 3 exchanges * 8 g = 24 g protein.
3. Salad greens: 1 cup raw leafy vegetables = 1 exchange Vegetable Group A/B = 1 g protein.
4. Banana: 1 exchange Fruit = 0 g protein.
Total Protein = 3 g (rice) + 24 g (chicken) + 1 g (greens) + 0 g (fruit) = 28 gm.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. 28 gm. Margin calculation: 3g (1.5 ex rice) + 24g (3 ex meat) + 1g (1 ex veg) = 28 gm.

cards.front: Plain, cool water is the best fluid for everyday active people because it _____.
cards.back: B. rapidly leaves the digestive tract to enter the tissues and cool the body
options: A. leaves the digestive tract slowly
B. rapidly leaves the digestive tract to enter the tissues and cool the body
cards.rationale: Cool or chilled water (around 10-15°C / 50-59°F) empties from the stomach significantly faster than warm fluids or concentrated hypertonic beverages, promoting rapid intestinal absorption to restore plasma volume while helping lower core body temperature during physical activity.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. rapidly leaves the digestive tract to enter the tissues and cool the body.

cards.front: Example of medication-related symptoms that will most likely and significantly limit food intake include _____.
options: B. skin rash and ringing in the ear
cards.rationale: Severe, persistent nausea and vomiting directly incapacitate the patient's physiological ability to consume, tolerate, and retain oral food and liquids, leading to acute hypovolemia, electrolyte disturbances, and rapid nutritional decline.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. persistent nausea and vomiting. Major drug-induced nutrition impact symptom.

cards.front: Diet management for Congestive Heart Failure include the following interventions. Which one is prohibited because it can provoke cardiac arrythmia?
options: A. Take small but frequent meals
cards.rationale: Excessive caffeine (a central nervous system and cardiac beta-adrenergic stimulant) and heavy alcohol intake can precipitate tachyarrhythmias, atrial fibrillation ('holiday heart syndrome'), and myocardial depression in patients with compromised cardiac function and heart failure.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. No caffeine, no alcohol. Caffeine and alcohol provoke cardiac arrhythmias.

cards.front: Much of these nutrients is the LEAST affected during stress _____.
cards.rationale: During acute metabolic stress (sepsis, trauma, burns), hypermetabolism causes profound alterations in glucose turnover (hyperglycemia), amino acid mobilization (accelerated muscle proteolysis), and fluid/electrolyte balance. Fat-soluble Vitamin E has extensive adipose and hepatic stores and its turnover is least acutely altered during acute stress.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. vitamin E. Water, glucose, and amino acid fluxes are massively affected during stress.

cards.front: Fluid balance is an aspect of the homeostasis of organisms which the concentration of electrolytes are kept at a healthy level. The state of body fluid volume balance is _____.
cards.rationale: Euvolemia refers to the optimal, physiologically normal circulating blood and extracellular fluid volume in the human body, balancing fluid intake and excretory outputs.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. euvolemia. Normal body fluid volume status.

cards.front: Which of the following describes fat soluble vitamins?
cards.back: A. Can be stored in the liver and fatty tissues and can reach toxic levels.
options: A. Can be stored in the liver and fatty tissues and can reach toxic levels.
B. It includes Vit A and Vit. C
C. Can't be stored to any great extent so must be consumed daily.
D. Toxic levels can be reached by consuming citrus fruits and vegetables.
cards.rationale: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) are absorbed along with dietary lipids via mixed micelles and chylomicrons and are stored extensively in hepatic tissue and adipose reserves. Because they are not readily excreted in urine, excessive chronic intakes can accumulate to toxic levels (hypervitaminosis A or D).
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. Can be stored in the liver and fatty tissues and can reach toxic levels.

cards.front: Patients with calcium oxalate stones may benefit from diet that restrict:
cards.rationale: In calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis, high sodium intake reduces renal tubular reabsorption of calcium, causing hypercalciuria, while excessive dietary oxalate increases urinary oxalate concentration. Restricting oxalate-rich foods (spinach, rhubarb, beets, chocolate, nuts) and maintaining low sodium (<2,000 mg/day) with normal dietary calcium intake (which binds oxalate in the gut) prevents stone recurrence.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. oxalate and sodium. Note: Calcium should NOT be restricted; restrict oxalate and sodium.

cards.front: The hormone that moves milk through the mammary gland?
cards.rationale: Oxytocin, secreted by the posterior pituitary, stimulates the contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the mammary alveoli to eject milk into the lactiferous ducts ('let-down reflex' or milk ejection). In contrast, prolactin stimulates milk production/synthesis.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. Oxytocin. Oxytocin = milk ejection/let-down; Prolactin = milk production.

cards.front: In celiac disease, a fraction of the protein gluten in wheat and corresponding protein fractions in barley, oats and rye:
cards.back: B. acts as toxic substance and called the intestinal villi to lose their absorptive capacity
options: A. are clearly marked on food labels when they are used in food products
B. acts as toxic substance and called the intestinal villi to lose their absorptive capacity
C. allow oxalate to be absorbed and contribute to higher incidence of oxalate kidney stones
D. blinds fats and calcium so that they cannot be absorbed
cards.rationale: In Celiac Disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy), proline- and glutamine-rich prolamin peptides (gliadin in wheat, secalin in rye, hordein in barley) trigger an autoimmune inflammatory reaction in the lamina propria, causing intraepithelial lymphocytosis, crypt hyperplasia, and severe villous atrophy with loss of absorptive surface area.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. acts as toxic substance and called the intestinal villi to lose their absorptive capacity.

cards.front: One of the typical treatment symptoms of food allergies is;
cards.rationale: The only definitive, primary management and therapy for confirmed IgE- or non-IgE-mediated food allergies is strict, lifelong elimination of the culprit food allergen from the patient's diet.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. elimination of the allergen. Strict avoidance/elimination is the cornerstone of food allergy therapy.

cards.front: Which fat-soluble vitamin if lacking, can cause impaired vision in reduced light?
cards.rationale: Vitamin A (retinol/retinal) combines with the protein opsin in retinal rod cells to form rhodopsin (visual purple), the light-sensitive visual pigment responsible for vision in dim light. Vitamin A deficiency impairs rhodopsin regeneration, causing nyctalopia (night blindness).
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. Retinol. Margin note: 'ADEK'. Retinal forms rhodopsin for scotopic (dim light) vision.

cards.front: Heat syndrome results when the body's production of heat increases at a faster rate than the body's ability to dissipate heat loss. Which of the following is the type of heat syndrome in its most severe from?
cards.rationale: Heat stroke is the most severe and life-threatening heat-related medical emergency. It is characterized by thermoregulatory failure resulting in a core body temperature > 40°C (104°F), central nervous system dysfunction (delirium, convulsions, coma), and multiorgan failure.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. Heat stroke. Life-threatening heat illness with core temp > 40°C and CNS dysfunction.

cards.front: When monitoring for food allergy, which outcome should be measured?
cards.back: D. reduction of food related reactions
options: B. level of knowledges about causes of food allergies
C. frequency of patient failure to comply with instruction
D. reduction of food related reactions
cards.rationale: In the Nutrition Care Process (NCP) for food allergies, the primary clinical outcome measure to monitor and evaluate is the reduction or complete cessation of adverse food-related allergic reactions following allergen elimination.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. reduction of food related reactions. Primary clinical efficacy outcome in allergy management.

cards.front: Because its nitrogenous wastes contribute to uremia, the following nutrient may be restricted in diets of renal clients
cards.rationale: Dietary protein catabolism generates nitrogenous metabolic end-products, including urea, creatinine, uric acid, guanidines, and phenolic compounds. In non-dialyzed chronic kidney disease, dietary protein is controlled/restricted (0.6–0.8 g/kg/day) to decrease nitrogenous waste accumulation, relieve uremic symptoms, and slow renal progression.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. Protein. Nitrogenous waste products from protein catabolism drive uremic toxicity.

cards.front: Which of these exchanges does not contain protein?
cards.rationale: In the Food Exchange Lists (PEL), 1 Fat exchange contains 0 g Carbohydrate, 0 g Protein, and 5 g Fat (45 kcal). In contrast, Low-fat milk provides 8 g protein, Vegetable provides 1 g (Group A) or 2 g (Group B) protein, and Bread/Rice provides 2 g protein per exchange.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. Fat. Fat exchange = 0g CHO, 0g PRO, 5g FAT (45 kcal).

cards.front: Giving cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents produces all of the following nutrition impact symptoms, EXCEPT:
cards.rationale: Cytotoxic antineoplastic drugs rapidly damage rapidly dividing epithelial cells, producing signature nutrition impact symptoms: nausea, vomiting, profound anorexia, dysgeusia, oral mucositis, and diarrhea. Hypotension is a cardiovascular/hemodynamic sign rather than a classic direct nutrition impact symptom.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. hypotension. Nutrition impact symptoms directly interfere with dietary intake and digestion.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a function of the kidney?
I. Formation of the plasma protein
II. Regulates the blood pressure
III. Stimulates the red blood cell production
IV. Activates Vitamin D
cards.rationale: The kidneys regulate blood pressure via the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (II), stimulate erythropoiesis by synthesizing erythropoietin (III), and perform the final 1-alpha-hydroxylation of 25(OH)D to active calcitriol (IV). Synthesis of plasma proteins (albumin, fibrinogen, transferrin) is performed by the liver, not the kidneys (I is incorrect).
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: B. II, III & IV. Renal functions: BP regulation (renin), RBC production (EPO), Vit D activation (calcitriol).

cards.front: Which of the following list of symptoms are systemic?
cards.back: D. Headache, irritability, arrythmia, low BP
options: D. Headache, irritability, arrythmia, low BP
cards.rationale: Systemic symptoms affect multiple body systems simultaneously or involve widespread neuro-hemodynamic responses. Headache, neuro-irritability, cardiac arrhythmias, and arterial hypotension represent generalized cardiovascular and systemic manifestations, whereas the other options are organ-specific (respiratory, GI, cutaneous).
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. Headache, irritability, arrythmia, low BP. Systemic hemodynamic and neurological manifestations.

cards.front: One specific indication of enteral nutrition is:
cards.rationale: Enteral nutrition support is indicated when a patient has a functioning, accessible gastrointestinal tract but cannot or will not consume adequate oral nutrition (such as in severe prolonged anorexia nervosa, hypercatabolic cancer anorexia, or neurological dysphagia). Small bowel obstruction, severe intractable diarrhea, and active upper GI bleeding are absolute contraindications to enteral feeding.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. anorexia. Gut works? Use it! A, B, and D are absolute contraindications to enteral nutrition.

cards.front:
Diet management for Dumping Syndrome includes:
I. Small meals spread out throughout the day
II. High protein, moderate fat foods are recommended
III. Small amount of simple sugar may be taken as tolerated
IV. Use of fiber supplement to reduce upper GI transit time and decrease glucose absorption
options: A. I, II, III and IV
cards.rationale: Dumping syndrome MNT emphasizes: (I) small, frequent meals spread over 5–6 feedings, (II) high protein and moderate fat to slow gastric emptying and sustain satiety, and (III) strictly limiting concentrated simple sugars (taking only small tolerated amounts). Regarding IV: Soluble fiber *increases* (delays) upper GI transit time rather than reducing it.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. I, II and III. Dumping syndrome: small frequent meals, high protein, moderate fat, restricted sweets.

cards.front:
Some RND's have been successful using the following approaches to make their interaction with difficult clients easier. Which will work BEST?
I. Giving assignment prior to next session.
II. Requesting for return demo after instruction was given.
III. Summarize the patient's main concern and offer feedback of what you heard.
IV. Give a strong impression that your instructions should be followed.
options: B. I, II, III, and IV
cards.rationale: Effective client-centered counseling uses active listening (summarizing concerns and reflective feedback - III), behavioral assignments/homework (I), and return demonstration/teach-back to verify competence (II). Authoritarian demands (IV - 'give a strong impression that instructions must be followed') provoke resistance and damage therapeutic rapport.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. I, II, and III. Reflective listening, teach-back, and self-monitoring assignments build rapport.

cards.front:
Which is responsible for regulating the acidic environment in the stomach?
I. Gastrin
II. Nerve receptor
III. Secretin
IV. Hydrochloric Acid
cards.rationale: Gastric acid secretion is tightly regulated by: Gastrin (I, secreted by antral G-cells, strongly stimulates parietal acid secretion), Neural receptors (II, vagal cholinergic and histamine H2 receptors), and Secretin (III, released by duodenal S-cells in response to acid, inhibits gastrin release and parietal cell acid secretion while stimulating pancreatic bicarbonate). Hydrochloric acid (IV) is the secretory product itself, not a regulatory controller.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: A. I, II and III. Regulators of acid secretion: Gastrin (+), Vagal/ACh/Histamine (+), Secretin (-).

cards.front: The difference between cis and trans fatty acid is the _____.
cards.back: C. configuration of the double bond
options: A. location of their first double
B. number of their double bonds
C. configuration of the double bond
D. length of their carbon chain
cards.rationale: Cis and trans fatty acid isomers differ in the spatial geometric configuration of hydrogen atoms across the carbon-carbon double bond. In cis configuration, hydrogen atoms are on the same side, creating a kink/bend in the hydrocarbon chain. In trans configuration, hydrogen atoms are on opposite sides, producing a linear, rigid conformation similar to saturated fatty acids.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. configuration of the double bond. Cis = same side (kinked); Trans = opposite sides (straight).

cards.front: A Sports ND is usually consulted for tips to boost performance before a game. Which of the following should NOT be a part of your advice?
cards.back: C. It's alright to try new foods on race or game day.
options: A. Carbohydrate is very important as the body needs it to fuel the working muscle.
B. Protein is important for building and repair of muscle tissues.
C. It's alright to try new foods on race or game day.
D. Give fluid prescription on how much to drink before, during and after a game.
cards.rationale: A cardinal, non-negotiable rule in sports nutrition is 'never try anything new on competition or game day.' Introducing unfamiliar foods, supplements, or high-fiber foods immediately prior to an athletic event risks sudden severe gastrointestinal upset, diarrhea, nausea, and cramping.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: C. It's alright to try new foods on race or game day. Golden rule in sports nutrition: Never experiment on race day.

cards.front: A patient is MOST likely to experience nausea, vomiting, bloating, increased flatus after suddenly changing from low to high dietary intake of:
cards.rationale: Abruptly increasing dietary fiber intake without a gradual step-up and without adequate fluid intake causes undigested polysaccharides to enter the colon rapidly, where anaerobic colonic bacteria undergo rapid fermentation, generating large volumes of hydrogen, methane, and carbon dioxide gases (bloating, cramping, and flatus).
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. fiber. Rapid escalation of dietary fiber causes severe gas and abdominal distension.

cards.front: Dr. Santos referred his hypertensive pt for diet counseling with a prescription for a low sodium diet. How many mg of sodium is allowed on this diet?
cards.rationale: In standard clinical dietetics and hospital diet manuals, a standard 'low sodium diet' (or mild/moderate sodium restriction) prescribes 2,000 mg of sodium daily (equivalent to approximately 5 grams of table salt). Strict sodium diets (500-1,000 mg) are rarely prescribed due to poor palatability and risk of hyponatremia.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. 2,000 mg (C. 1,000 mg also noted for moderate restriction; 2,000 mg is standard clinical target).

cards.front: Refeeding syndrome causes dangerous fluctuations in:
cards.rationale: Refeeding syndrome is characterized by rapid, life-threatening shifts in serum electrolytes—principally acute hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia—triggered by carbohydrate re-introduction and insulin release driving electrolytes into cells for glucose phosphorylation and protein synthesis.
cards.userNotes: Exam marked: D. electrolytes. Critical electrolyte shifts (PO4, K, Mg) cause cardiac arrhythmias.

cards.front:
Which of these are the functions of the kidney?
I. Formation of plasma protein
II. Regulates blood pressure
III. Stimulates red blood cell production
IV. Activates Vit. D
